Empty-Net Goals in NHL Betting: How They Swing Totals

Published October 21, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

With about ninety seconds left and a one-goal deficit, an NHL coach pulls the goalie for an extra attacker. Fans watching at home mostly care whether their team scores. Bettors with money on the total, the puck line, or a live moneyline are watching a completely different game, because that single tactical decision — not a shift in talent or momentum — is one of the biggest volatility events left in a hockey betting slip. Roughly one out of every nine or ten NHL games produces at least one empty-net goal, and the way that goal gets scored changes several markets at once, often within the same ninety-second window.

In this guide

  1. Why pulling the goalie creates a scoring spike, not just a risk
  2. What it does to the live total
  3. What it does to the puck line and moneyline

Why pulling the goalie creates a scoring spike, not just a risk

Most bettors understand the obvious part: an empty net is easier to score into than a guarded one, so the trailing team's odds of scoring go up. What's less obvious is that the leading team's odds of scoring also go up, sometimes by more. Once the opposing net is empty, the leading team doesn't need to beat a goaltender to extend the lead — an empty-net goal from center ice as the trailing team pushes for the tying score is one of the single easiest goals in hockey to score, if the leading team can just get the puck and a clear shooting lane. That's why six-on-five situations frequently end with more total goals scored in the final two minutes than the rest of the period combined, even though only one team is actually trying to score against a goaltender.

This matters for betting because it means the empty-net stretch isn't simply "more variance for the trailing team." It's a genuine increase in the expected number of goals in the game, full stop, which is exactly the kind of thing a total or a live moneyline has to price.

What it does to the live total

If you're holding a live bet on the total, or considering one once a goalie gets pulled, the number you're looking at should move meaningfully in that window. A six-on-five situation in the final two minutes effectively adds a mini-overtime's worth of goal-scoring opportunity on top of a game that was already going to finish regardless. Sportsbooks that offer live markets adjust the remaining-time total upward the moment a goalie comes off, and the adjustment tends to be larger than casual bettors expect — it's not unusual for the implied goal rate in that stretch to be three or four times the per-minute rate from earlier in the game.

Takeaway: A pulled goalie isn't a minor variable at the edge of a totals bet — for the two minutes it lasts, it's one of the highest-scoring-rate situations the sport produces, and live lines are built to reflect that, not to lag behind it.

What it does to the puck line and moneyline

For a pre-game puck line (typically 1.5 goals) or moneyline, the empty-net stretch is where a lot of games that looked settled stop being settled. A team up by one goal with two minutes left is in a far less secure position than the same lead with two minutes left in, say, an NFL game, because the trailing team is about to deliberately increase the variance of the remainder of the game. Covering a 1.5-goal favorite moneyline becomes meaningfully less certain in exactly this window, and a live moneyline on the trailing team can still carry real value even down a goal with 90 seconds left, specifically because of how often six-on-five results in a quick answer.

MarketEffect once the goalie is pulled
Live totalMoves up sharply for the remaining time; implied goal rate spikes
Live moneyline (trailing team)Improves faster than the raw time remaining would suggest
Puck line / spreadA 1-goal lead becomes less secure than the same lead earlier in the game
Pre-game total (settled)An empty-net goal counts fully; one extra goal can flip an Over/Under that looked decided

Empty-net goals and player props

An empty-net goal is scored exactly like any other goal for the purposes of a player's goal or point props, and that detail matters a lot for a favorite's leading scorers sitting one shy of the Over on a goals or points prop late in a lopsided game. It's a common live-betting angle: once the trailing team pulls its goalie, a star player already on the ice for the leading team is in unusually favorable position to add an easy stat-padding goal or assist into an empty net, and some books shade in-game player prop lines accordingly in the final minutes of a game that's already decided on the scoreboard but not yet on the clock.

Why some teams pull the goalie earlier than others

The classic "pull the goalie with a minute left" instinct has shifted over the past decade. Advanced-stats-driven coaching staffs increasingly pull goalies down a goal with as much as two and a half to three minutes left, because modeling shows the expected value of extra offensive-zone time outweighs the small added risk of conceding an extra empty-net goal against. Teams and coaches that lean on this research tend to create longer, earlier six-on-five stretches than a more traditional staff waiting until the final 60 seconds — which means the "when does the volatility window open" question isn't identical from team to team, and it's worth knowing which benches tend to pull early when you're tracking a live total.

Mistakes bettors make around empty-net situations

  • Treating a one-goal lead late as settled. It's a meaningfully less secure lead than the scoreboard alone suggests, specifically because of what the trailing team is about to do.
  • Betting a live total without accounting for the spike. The per-minute goal rate in a six-on-five stretch isn't a small step up from the rest of the game — treating it that way underprices the number.
  • Ignoring which team's goalie gets pulled first in overlapping situations. Rare late-game sequences where both teams briefly empty their nets (a delayed penalty on the trailing team while their goalie is already off) multiply the scoring-rate effect further and are easy to misjudge in the moment.
  • Forgetting that empty-net goals count fully for props and totals. Some bettors mentally discount a "garbage time" empty-netter as if it doesn't really count — it settles exactly the same as any other goal on the books.
Live betting during an empty-net stretch moves fast and the number can shift several times in under a minute. If you're betting in-play late in a close game, decide your limit before the goalie comes off rather than chasing the line as it updates. Frequently asked questions

Does an empty-net goal count toward a goalie's save percentage?

No. An empty-net goal is not credited as a shot against the goaltender who was pulled, since they weren't on the ice to face it. It does count as a goal for team and player scoring statistics, including props.

How often do empty-net goals actually happen in an NHL game?

Estimates vary by season, but roughly one in every nine or ten NHL games features at least one empty-net goal — common enough that it's a regular factor in late-game totals and moneylines, not a rare fluke.

Do sportsbooks stop taking live bets once a goalie is pulled?

Usually not entirely, but many books widen the margin or briefly suspend specific markets while they reprice for the sudden change in scoring probability, then reopen betting at adjusted numbers within seconds.

Does pulling the goalie actually work more often than it backfires?

Analytics-driven research generally supports pulling the goalie earlier than old-school convention suggested, on the logic that the extra offensive-zone time created outweighs the added empty-net risk — but it still fails to produce a tying goal considerably more often than it succeeds, since trailing by a goal with limited time remains a tough spot regardless of tactics.
